rows.question: Name the areas of high-risk use cases. Is healthcare decision making one of them?
rows.answer: No, "healthcare decision-making" is not itself one of the high-risk areas. Annex III lists eight areas: biometrics (Annex III.1); critical infrastructure (Annex III.2); education and vocational training (Annex III.3); employment, workers management and access to self-employment (Annex III.4); access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits (Annex III.5); law enforcement (Annex III.6); migration, asylum and border control management (Annex III.7); and administration of justice and democratic processes (Annex III.8). Under Article 6(2) only a listed lettered use-case within those areas makes a system high-risk, so clinical decision-making as such is outside the list. Healthcare nonetheless appears as specific use-cases: evaluating eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, and granting, reducing, revoking or reclaiming them (Annex III.5(a)); risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance (Annex III.5(c)); and evaluating and classifying emergency calls, dispatching or prioritising emergency first response, including medical aid, and emergency healthcare patient triage (Annex III.5(d)). Separately, clinical AI is high-risk by the Annex I product route under Article 6(1) where it is a medical device or a safety component of one requiring third-party conformity assessment (Annex I.11 to 12).
criteria_text: Biometrics; Critical infrastructure; Education and vocational training; Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; Access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services and benefits; Law enforcement; Migration, asylum and border control management; Administration of justice and democratic processes
No
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer lists all eight areas from Annex III, matching the substance of criterion 1 using different but equivalent phrasing.
The candidate answer unambiguously states 'No' at the beginning and maintains that position, explaining why general healthcare decision-making is not a listed high-risk area under Annex III.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; logically organised and actionable for a compliance audience.

rows.question: Could the introduction of guardrails in an AI agentic system reduce the risk of the system from high risk to moderate risk? What about changing the capabilities and intended use of the system?
rows.answer: No. Guardrails do not move a system out of the high-risk class: classification under Article 6(2) turns on whether the system falls within a listed Annex III use-case (or, under Article 6(1), is a safety component of, or a product covered by, Annex I legislation subject to third-party conformity assessment), and the Act recognises no "moderate risk" tier. Mitigation measures are instead the consequence of high-risk status, Article 8(1) requires compliance with Chapter III Section 2 taking account of intended purpose and state of the art, with the Article 9 risk-management system taken into account; guardrails are documented as risk-management and human-oversight measures in the Annex IV technical documentation and reflected in the Article 12(2) logging traceability and the Article 13(3)(b) statement of characteristics, capabilities and limitations, intended purpose, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, foreseeable risk circumstances, explanatory capabilities, performance for specific groups, input-data specifications and output-interpretation information. Changing capabilities and intended purpose can change classification, because intended purpose drives the Article 6 test, and Article 6(3) exempts systems posing no significant risk that perform only a narrow procedural, human-result-improving, pattern-detecting or preparatory task, unless profiling occurs. Such a change may make the modifier a provider under Article 25(1).
criteria_text: No - guardrails alone do not create an intermediate "moderate risk" tier; the Act's Article 6(3) derogation is binary (high-risk or exempted)

Exemption applies only where the system's intended task itself meets one of four Article 6(3) conditions: narrow procedural task; improving a previously completed human activity; detecting deviations from prior decisions without replacing human assessment; or a preparatory task
Yes - changing the system's capabilities/intended use can exit high-risk status if the redefined task now satisfies one of those conditions
Exception: an AI system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, regardless of guardrails or intended-use changes
criterion_remarks: The answer correctly states that guardrails do not create a moderate risk tier and that the classification is binary under Article 6(3), aligning with the substance of the criterion.

The answer identifies the four conditions in Article 6(3) by substance—narrow procedural, improving human results, detecting patterns without replacing assessment, and preparatory tasks—using different but equivalent phrasing.
The answer confirms that changing capabilities and intended use can affect classification if the new purpose meets one of the Article 6(3) conditions, which matches the criterion's substance.
The answer explicitly notes the exception for profiling, stating that such systems are always high-risk, satisfying the final criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear regulatory prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
rows.answer: Yes, the use is permitted. Generating and showing synthetic dermatological images for teaching is not among the practices prohibited by Article 5(1), and illustrative classroom use is not itself a listed Annex III use-case. Disclosure is nevertheless required where the images constitute a "deep fake" within Article 3(60), content resembling existing persons that would falsely appear authentic: the university, as deployer, must disclose that the content is artificially generated or manipulated under Article 50(4), first subparagraph. The provider must separately mark the output in a machine-readable, detectable format under Article 50(2). The lighter regime does not apply. The only relevant attenuation in Article 50(4), third subparagraph, is for content forming part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work; the law-enforcement carve-out covers only use authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences.
criteria_text: Yes, permitted
Disclosure still required under Article 50(4)
Lighter regime applies as "analogous work" to artistic/creative/fictional content — only existence of generated content must be disclosed, without hampering display/enjoyment
Law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and is inapplicable here
criterion_remarks: The answer states that the use is permitted and explains it is not prohibited under Article 5(1) or listed in Annex III.
The answer explicitly states that disclosure is required under Article 50(4), first subparagraph, for deep fakes resembling real persons.
The answer states the lighter regime does not apply, contradicting the criterion that it does apply as an analogous work.
The answer correctly distinguishes the law-enforcement carve-out as a full exemption and notes it is inapplicable here.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?
rows.answer: No. On these facts the tool is neither prohibited nor high-risk. Article 5(1)(d) prohibits AI making risk assessments to predict a natural person's commission of a criminal offence based solely on profiling or on assessing personality traits and characteristics; it expressly does not apply to AI supporting human assessment of involvement in criminal activity that is already based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to that activity, current-cart and checkout anomalies are such facts, and staff retain the optional manual bag check. Article 5(1)(c) is likewise unengaged: there is no evaluation over a certain period of time yielding a social score, no detriment in an unrelated social context, and no treatment disproportionate to the behaviour. No Annex III use-case, including the law-enforcement area reserved to law enforcement authorities, covers a retailer's own loss-prevention check.
criteria_text: No
Annex III.6 categories apply only where the AI system is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions/bodies in support of law enforcement authorities)

A supermarket's own loss-prevention/bag-check tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III.6 regardless of its resemblance to investigative or evaluative functions
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'No' as its clear position, matching the required verdict.
The answer explains that no Annex III use-case applies because the tool is used by a retailer, not by or on behalf of law enforcement, capturing the substance of the criterion.
The answer explicitly states that a retailer's loss-prevention tool run by store staff falls outside Annex III.6, directly conveying the substance of the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents a coherent regulatory analysis.

rows.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
rows.answer: No. The requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 continue to apply in full to the operator's AI safety component, and opting out of third-party assessment does not release you from them. Under Article 6(1), an AI system used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in the twenty acts spanning machinery, toys, recreational craft, lifts, ATEX equipment, radio equipment, pressure equipment, cableways, PPE, gas appliances, medical devices, in vitro diagnostics, civil aviation security, two- and three-wheel vehicles, agricultural and forestry vehicles, marine equipment, rail interoperability, motor vehicle type-approval, vehicle general safety, and civil aviation, is high-risk where that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment. Article 43(3) is decisive: where a Section A Annex I act lets the manufacturer opt out of third-party assessment on the basis of full application of harmonised standards, that option may be used only if the manufacturer has also applied harmonised standards or, where applicable, common specifications referred to in Article 41 covering all Section 2 requirements. The Article 43(1) internal-control/notified-body routes (points (a), (d)) govern Annex III point 1 systems, not the operator's Annex I product. The evidence supplied contains no text for the individual limbs of Article 41(1)(a)., so the precise conditions of that provision cannot be verified here.
criteria_text: No
Section 2 requirements still apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment (Art. 43(3), second sentence)
The third-party opt-out under sectoral legislation is available only if harmonised standards/common specifications applied cover ALL Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No' as the position, matching the required verdict.
The answer states that Section 2 requirements continue to apply and form part of the conformity assessment under Article 43(3), conveying the substance of the criterion.
The answer explains that the opt-out is available only if harmonised standards or common specifications cover all Section 2 requirements, which matches the substance of the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Inappropriate due to self-referential statement about 'evidence supplied' and inability to verify Article 41(1)(a), which introduces meta-commentary about the response process and limitations.
